detail.scope: Commercial-sector electricity sales and average price by state, as reported to EIA. Data centers are billed mostly in the commercial class, so this is a proxy for their load, not a measurement of it.

sources.name: ERCOT

sources.scope: Generator interconnection requests across the south-central US, all statuses as SPP publishes them, withdrawn requests counted separately.

sources.scope: Active generator interconnection requests on the California ISO grid, from the public queue report. Completed and withdrawn projects are counted separately.

analysis.body:
The five grid operators shown here — ERCOT, NYISO, MISO, Southwest Power Pool, and CAISO — each publish their own interconnection queue covering different geographic footprints and using different counting rules, so their totals cannot simply be added together. As of August 30, 2026, ERCOT's Texas queue alone lists 1,797 requests totaling roughly 440,018 MW of planned generation and storage, with solar at about 151,883 MW and battery storage at about 160,906 MW leading the mix; gas sits at 76,751 MW. NYISO's New York queue shows 1,414 requests for roughly 319,095 MW, though the overwhelming majority — about 291,136 MW — falls in an "other" category as NYISO publishes it, with gas at 27,879 MW. MISO's 3,827 requests cover about 255,226 MW across the Midcontinent, led by solar at 117,482 MW, wind at 44,641 MW, and storage at 37,129 MW, with gas at 28,645 MW. SPP's 1,078 requests total roughly 199,215 MW in the south-central US, where wind at 64,737 MW and storage at 53,412 MW are joined by a notable 47,392 MW of gas. CAISO's active California queue is the smallest shown, at 265 requests and about 71,682 MW, dominated by storage at 46,944 MW and solar at 18,896 MW, with gas at only 916 MW.

These queue figures represent planned projects waiting to connect to the grid, not data center electricity demand itself, and most will never reach commercial operation. That said, for readers tracking AI infrastructure, the growth of battery storage and gas-peaker requests is the relevant signal: storage fills in the gap when intermittent renewables cannot meet the continuous, around-the-clock load profile that large data centers impose, and gas provides firm capacity for the same reason. Storage requests are substantial in every queue that reports them separately — 160,906 MW in ERCOT, 53,412 MW in SPP, 46,944 MW in CAISO, and 37,129 MW in MISO — and gas requests remain significant in ERCOT, SPP, and MISO, the three regions where large-scale data center campus development has been most active. The commercial electricity sales data reported to EIA for June 2026 show Texas leading all states listed at 15,754 GWh, followed by California at 10,025 GWh and Virginia at 7,771 GWh; Virginia's figure is particularly notable given that commercial sales there are reported at an average price of $10.99 per kWh while the state hosts the world's densest concentration of data center capacity.

Prices vary considerably across the states in the EIA data: California's commercial rate of $27.33 per kWh is more than three times Texas's $8.66, which helps explain why Texas continues to attract the largest volume of new interconnection requests despite already carrying a massive existing queue. Watch for ERCOT's monthly Generator Interconnection Status report to see whether the storage-to-gas ratio in new requests shifts over the coming quarters, since a sustained rise in gas requests relative to storage would be the clearest early sign that grid planners expect firm, dispatchable power needs — the kind driven by always-on computing loads — to outpace what storage alone can meet.
